structure.overview: Ms. Kifungo seeks judicial review of an Immigration Officer's refusal to grant her permanent residence in Canada under humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds. The Immigration Officer found her evidence on establishment in Canada, family ties, and country conditions insufficient and dismissed her claim as unreasonable. The Federal Court upheld the Officer's decision, finding it reasonable and supported by the evidence, and dismissed the judicial review application.

party_points.text: Officer failed to apply section 25 H&C considerations
Officer fettered discretion by not examining hardship if returned to Congo
Applicant incapable of leaving Canada due to moratorium
Claim to help raise nephew supported by evidence

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Ms. Kifungo seeks judicial review of an Immigration Officer's refusal to grant permanent residence without applying section 25 H&C considerations.

citations.cite: section 11 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA]
citations.why: Legal requirement for application from outside Canada
Section allowing H&C considerations for permanent residence

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant and her brother entered Canada in August 2010; she is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant and siblings crossed the US/Canada border to seek refugee status; the older sister was refused entry due to age, Applicant was 16.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant's parents' situation in Congo is unclear; her father was detained twice and later left for Gabon; mother stayed in Congo.

citations.why: Court decision on asylum refusal mentioning father's detention

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The judicial review of the Applicant's asylum claim was dismissed; the RPD found lack of credibility, confirmed by the Court as reasonable.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Submissions before the Immigration Officer focused on Applicant's establishment in Canada, length of stay, and risks if returned to Congo, not survival details.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Senior Immigration Officer found the Applicant's establishment in Canada lacked substance despite nearly 10 years' stay, citing Irimie on H&C test.
idea_list: Citation of Irimie case on H&C test

citations.cite: Irimie v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2000 CanLII 16640 (FC) [Irimie]
citations.why: Defines H&C test not as immigration screening

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer cited Kanthasamy to note hardship of leaving Canada alone is insufficient for relief under section 25(1) IRPA, referencing Irimie again.

citations.cite: Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61, [2015] 3 SCR 909 [Kanthasamy]
citations.why: Hardship alone insufficient for relief under section 25(1)
Referenced by Kanthasamy on hardship

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer rejected the Applicant's argument that a moratorium on removals prevented her from leaving Canada, stating it is a shield, not a sword.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer corrected the Applicant's impression that she was obligated to stay in Canada due to the moratorium, stating she was free to leave.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer noted limited financial information from the Applicant, especially no details from 2010 to 2016 on how she subsisted in Canada.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer found little evidence on education and community involvement, concluding the Applicant's establishment and ties in Canada were unclear.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer reviewed Congo's difficult conditions but found the Applicant's evidence on family and country situation vague and insufficient, citing Owusu.
idea_list: Cites Owusu on responsibility for evidence

citations.cite: Owusu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FCA 38, [2004] 2 FCR 635 [Owusu]
citations.why: Applicant responsible for providing evidence

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer considered the best interests of the Applicant's nephew, noting limited contact and financial support from the Applicant.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer found insufficient evidence about the nephew to justify relief under section 25(1), concluding combined grounds did not warrant exemption.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court sympathizes but finds the Applicant's evidence before the Officer fatally defective, so the decision's reasonableness stands.

citations.why: Judicial review based on record before decision maker

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The parties agree the standard of review is reasonableness, confirmed by the Supreme Court in Vavilov as the presumption in all cases.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]
citations.why: Confirms reasonableness as presumptive standard

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Vavilov requires applicants to show unreasonableness; reasonableness demands justification, transparency, intelligibility; flaws include incoherence or unjustified conclusions.
idea_list: Burden on applicant to show unreasonableness

citations.why: Defines reasonableness requirements and flaws

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court must show judicial restraint, respect administrative roles, and not reweigh evidence or accept new evidence on review.

citations.why: Emphasizes judicial restraint and respect for administrative decisions

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer fettered discretion by not examining hardship if returned to Congo, but the record does not support this.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant argued she was incapable of leaving Canada due to moratorium; Officer misunderstood this as a creditable prevention from return.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer corrected the misunderstanding, acknowledged the moratorium, and linked it to a hypothetical return to Congo.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RPD can reject evidence based on implausibility and found the Applicant failed to prove fear of persecution; this was reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Contrary to Applicant's claim, the Officer considered the TSR and discussed hypothetical return if moratorium lifts, requiring application from outside Canada.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Relief varies by case, but H&C officers must consider all relevant facts substantively, citing Baker for this principle.

citations.why: Officers must consider all relevant facts in H&C determinations

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Due to the TSR, the Officer did not consider the Applicant at risk of removal; the Applicant failed to submit evidence on country conditions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's claim that the establishment analysis is unintelligible fails due to lack of evidence; affidavit after the fact is unhelpful.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's claim to help raise her nephew is unsupported by evidence; the Officer noted almost no information about the child.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer did not require hardship evidence but evidence about the child; lack of evidence was fatal to the Applicant's claim.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant failed to show the decision was unreasonable due to lack of evidence; Kanthasamy and Chirwa define H&C considerations as evidence-based.
idea_list: Kanthasamy and Chirwa define H&C evidence standard

citations.why: Defines H&C considerations as evidence-based

citations.cite: Chirwa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1970), 4 IAC 338
citations.why: Quoted on H&C considerations requiring evidence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The parties did not request certification of a question under section 74 of the IRPA, and the court agrees no such question arose.

citations.why: Refers to the statutory provision for certifying a question

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states that factual findings by the decision maker are generally not interfered with on review unless exceptional circumstances exist, citing multiple authorities.
idea_list: court defers to factual findings except in exceptional cases

citations.why: Supports deference to decision maker's factual findings
Supports deference to decision maker's factual findings
Supports deference to decision maker's factual findings

Explains reasons for deference to first instance findings

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains that a reasonable decision must be justified by facts and evidence, and unreasonableness arises if the decision maker misapprehends or ignores evidence, citing Dunsmuir and Baker.
idea_list: examples of unreasonableness from misapprehension of evidence

citations.why: Defines reasonable decision as justified by facts
Decision must consider evidentiary record and factual matrix
Example of unreasonableness from ignoring evidence and bias
